articles.title: A Gun Ruling Highlights the Tricks Congress Uses To Evade Limits on Its Power
articles.content:
上周，一名德克萨斯州的联邦法官裁定，几项全国性的枪支法规违宪，这一决定受到了第二修正案团体的欢迎。然而，这一裁决并不依赖于枪支权利，而是确认了一个更广泛的原则：联邦政府的权力仅限于宪法明确授予的权力。

这起案件涉及的是《国家枪支法》（NFA），该法于1934年通过，针对的是被认为是犯罪分子偏爱的武器和配件。由于该法被定义为一项税收措施，美国地区法院法官詹姆斯·亨德里克斯指出，国会通过取消对消音器、短管步枪和短管霰弹枪的制造和转让的联邦税收，削弱了该法某些条款的宪法依据，从而致命地破坏了这些条款的合法性。

国会去年通过了一项法律，保留了NFA对机枪和“破坏性装置”（如炸弹和手榴弹）的税收，但废除了对该法涉及的其他所有产品的税收。亨德里克斯法官认为，鉴于这一变化，对后一类产品的报告、登记和记录保存要求，原本旨在促进税收征收，但现在已不能再以国会在92年前通过该法时所援引的税收权力为由来加以合理化。

NFA作为《内部收入法典》的一部分，其合法性可能看起来有些古怪，因为国会长期以来一直依赖其对州际贸易的管辖权作为立法的万能许可证。但在1934年，立法者们认为，这种权力不足以授权对政治上不受欢迎的产品实施全面禁令，这种观点直到最高法院开始扭曲《商务条款》后才获得认可。

与直接禁止列举的武器不同，国会对其生产和转让征收了200美元的税收。这笔税收，相当于今天的5,000美元，旨在成为一种禁止性税收。

当时的司法部长霍默·卡明斯在支持NFA的证词中解释了这种迂回方法的必要性。尽管国会“显然”没有“固有的警察权力”可以进入某些地方处理当地犯罪问题，他说，但仍可以使用“税收权力”来限制那些被视为特别危险的武器。

“如果我们制定了一项法律，绝对禁止任何人拥有机枪，你可能会说涉及了一些宪法问题。但是，当你说‘我们将对机枪征税’，并且当你说没有许可证显示已缴纳税款表明犯罪行为发生时，你仍然在法律范围内。”卡明斯解释道。

国会在1914年批准的《哈里森鸦片税法》采取了类似的方法，该法案实际上禁止了鸦片和可卡因的非医疗用途。它同样依赖“税收权力”来为1937年大麻的事实全国禁令提供合法性。

最高法院在1928年祝福了这种借口，支持《哈里森法案》的理由是它产生了“实质性收入”，这与其广告目的一致。但亨德里克斯指出，当国会废除了大多数NFA管制产品的税收时，国会打破了这种脆弱的理由。

特朗普政府认为，NFA法规仍然可以通过《商务条款》得到合理化。亨德里克斯，作为特朗普任命的法官，不同意这一观点，认为政府“不能使用事后的合理化来挽救基于国会从未援引的列举权力的法律”。

如今，国会依赖《商务条款》来制定各种在过去被认为超出其范围的法规，包括那些既不是州际也不是商业的行为的刑事化法律。克拉伦斯·托马斯大法官在2005年涉及加州种植和消费医用大麻的案件中警告说：“如果国会可以根据《商务条款》管制这类事物，那么它几乎可以管制任何事情——联邦政府不再是一个受限制和列举权力的政府。”

亨德里克斯的决定是对这一基本原则的欢迎提醒。但自1934年以来，国会已经找到了一个新的借口来合理化它几乎想做的任何事情。
articles.summary:
Second Amendment groups applauded last week after a federal judge in Texas ruled that several national firearm regulations were unconstitutional. But the decision did not hinge on gun rights. Rather, it affirmed a broader principle: The federal government's powers are limited to those explicitly granted by the Constitution.

The case involved the National Firearms Act (NFA), a 1934 law that targeted weapons and accessories thought to be favored by criminals. Because that law was framed as a revenue measure, U.S. District Judge James Hendrix held, Congress fatally undermined the constitutional rationale for some of its provisions by eliminating the federal taxes on making and transferring sound suppressors, short-barreled rifles, and short-barreled shotguns.

Congress did that last year, when it approved a law that retained the NFA's taxes on machine guns and "destructive devices" such as bombs and grenades but repealed the taxes on all other products covered by the law. Given that change, Hendrix concluded, the reporting, registration, and record-keeping requirements for the latter set of products, which ostensibly were aimed at facilitating revenue collection, could no longer be justified by the tax power that Congress invoked when it passed the law 92 years ago.

That rationale for the NFA, which was enacted as part of the Internal Revenue Code, may seem puzzling, since Congress has long relied on its power to regulate interstate commerce as an all-purpose license to legislate. But in 1934, legislators did not think that power was broad enough to authorize outright bans on politically disfavored products, an idea that would not gain currency until after the Supreme Court began stretching the Commerce Clause beyond recognition.

Instead of banning the listed weapons, Congress imposed a $200 tax on their production and transfer. That tax, which is equivalent to about $5,000 today, was meant to be prohibitive.

Attorney General Homer Cummings explained the need for that roundabout approach when he testified in favor of the NFA. Although Congress "of course" had "no inherent police powers to go into certain localities and deal with local crime," he said, it could still use "the power of taxation" to restrict weapons it viewed as especially dangerous.

"If we made a statute absolutely forbidding any human being to have a machine gun," Cummings explained, "you might say there is some constitutional question involved. But when you say, 'We will tax the machine gun,' and when you say that the absence of a license showing payment of the tax has been made indicates that a crime has been perpetrated, you are easily within the law."

Congress had taken a similar approach when it approved the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act of 1914, which effectively prohibited nonmedical use of opiates and cocaine. It would likewise rely on "the power of taxation" to justify a de facto national ban on cannabis in 1937.

The Supreme Court blessed that pretext in 1928, upholding the Harrison Act on the grounds that it raised "substantial revenue," consistent with its advertised purpose. But as Hendrix noted, Congress broke that thin reed when it eliminated the taxes on most NFA-regulated products.

The Trump administration argued that the NFA regulations could still be justified under the Commerce Clause. Hendrix, a Trump appointee, disagreed, saying the government "cannot employ post-hoc justifications to save a statute based on an enumerated power that Congress never invoked."

Nowadays, of course, Congress relies on the Commerce Clause to enact all sorts of regulations that were once viewed as beyond its scope, including laws criminalizing conduct that is neither interstate nor commercial. "If Congress can regulate this under the Commerce Clause," Justice Clarence Thomas warned in a 2005 case involving medical marijuana grown and consumed in California, "then it can regulate virtually anything—and the Federal Government is no longer one of limited and enumerated powers."

Hendrix's decision is a welcome reminder of that fundamental principle. But since 1934, Congress has found a new excuse to justify almost anything it wants to do.

The post A Gun Ruling Highlights the Tricks Congress Uses To Evade Limits on Its Power appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: First Legal Challenges to Trump's New Birthright Citizenship Executive Order
articles.content:
几天前，我写了一篇文章讨论特朗普最近发布的生育公民权行政令，并解释了为何其绝大部分内容违宪。根据最高法院在"特朗普诉巴巴拉"案中的裁决，该裁决推翻了他早先的行政令，即剥夺未经授权移民和持临时签证者的子女的生育公民权。昨天和今天，针对新行政令的首两起法律挑战陆续提起。

这两起诉讼由挑战早期行政令的原告所提起。在"巴巴拉诉特朗普"案中，原告正在寻求修改针对早期行政令的禁令，或者颁布新的禁令，以明确指出他们不能根据新行政令被剥夺生育公民权。在"全美西班牙语会员协会诉特朗普"案中，原告正在寻求解除程序中止并召开状况会议，以讨论新行政令的问题。我预计他们最终也会寻求针对后者的禁令。

这两起案件均涉及集体诉讼，认定了一类将因特朗普最初的生育公民权行政令而失去公民身份的子女（即那些出生于非公民父母，这些父母或非法进入美国，或持有某种临时签证在美国）。集体诉讼认证是绕过最高法院去年在"全美西班牙语会员协会"案中不慎设立的全面禁令的重要工具之一。

我认为几乎所有受新行政令影响的人确实属于这两起案件中认证的类别，因为他们都是非公民父母的子女，这些父母要么非法进入美国，要么持有某种临时签证在美国。主要例外是出生于美属萨摩亚的儿童（即唯一受特朗普行政令中适用于"出生于美国领土或领海而不受联邦法规赋予公民身份"部分的人群），以及可能出生于为境外非公民订立合同的代孕母亲的儿童（这是特朗普行政令中关于"出生旅游"部分的内容）。美属萨摩亚出生的大多数婴儿——我假设——出生于该领土的永久合法居民。许多代孕母亲实际上可能是美国公民，而精子和卵子捐赠者（如果是非公民）可能从未踏足美国（无论是合法还是非法）。

使用这些早期案件来挑战新行政令可能会遇到各种程序障碍。其中一些程序问题超出了我的专业范围，因此我将留给其他人来解决。但我认为原告正确地指出了两点：1）新行政令显然是早期行政令的延续；2）其大部分内容在"特朗普诉巴巴拉"案中显然违宪。

此外，我认为州政府将能够挑战新行政令，就像一些州在下级法院针对早期行政令的挑战中取得成功一样。州政府提起的诉讼是获得普遍性（或至少非常广泛）禁令的另一种潜在途径，尤其是在"特朗普诉全美西班牙语会员协会"之后。去年，在"全美西班牙语会员协会"案之后，美国第九巡回上诉法院在一起挑战原始行政令的生育公民权案件中批准了这种禁令。

由于新行政令影响的人数远少于原始行政令，因此挑战它可能会面临更多的程序障碍。但我预计这些障碍最终会被克服，法院希望能够宣布其无效。当然，也会有关于相应禁令适用范围的争议。我认为普遍性禁令往往是有理由的。在"特朗普诉全美西班牙语会员协会"案之后，仍有各种途径可以获得它们（或者更准确地说，获得与它们非常相似的救济措施）。然而，最高法院迄今尚未给出明确的裁决，说明这些救济措施的可用性具体有多高。

该文章最初发表在Reason.com网站。
articles.summary:
A few days ago, I wrote about Trump's new birthright citizenship executive order and why the vast bulk of it is unconstitutional under the Supreme Court's ruling in Trump v. Barbara, which struck down his earlier executive order denying birthright citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants and those on temporary visas. Yesterday and today, the first two legal challenges to the new order were initiated.

They were filed by the plaintiffs in two of the cases challenging the earlier orders. The plaintiffs in Barbara v. Trump are seeking modification of the injunction against the earlier executive order or a new injunction making clear that they cannot be deprived of birthright citizenship under the new order. In CASA, Inc. v. Trump, the plaintiffs are seeking a lifting of the stay of proceedings and a status conference addressing the new order. I expect they, too, will eventually seek an injunction against the latter order.

Both cases involve class actions certifying a class of children who would lose citizenship under Trump's initial birthright citizenship order (those born to parents who are undocumented immigrants or non-citizens in the US on temporary visas). Class certifications are one of the tools available to get around the Supreme Court's unwise ban on universal injunctions established by its unwise ruling in the CASA case last year.

I think almost all of the people affected by the new order do, in fact, fit into the classes certified in these two cases, in the sense that they are all children of non-citizens who either entered the US illegally or are here on temporary visas of some kind. The principal exceptions are children born in American Samoa (the only people covered by the part of Trump's order applying to children "born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute"), and perhaps children born to surrogate mothers who contracted with noncitizens outside the US (this is an element of the part of Trump's order dealing with "birth tourism"). The vast majority of babies born in American Samoa are - I presume - born to permanent legal residents of that territory. Many of the surrogate mothers may actually be US citizens and the sperm and egg donors (if non-citizens) may not ever set foot in the United States at all (whether legally, or otherwise).

There may be various procedural obstacles to using these earlier cases to challenge the new executive order. Some of these procedural issues are outside my expertise, so I will have to leave them to others. But I do think the plaintiffs are right to point out 1) that the new order is clearly an outgrowth of the earlier one, and 2) much of it is clearly unconstitutional under Trump v. Barbara.

I expect, also, that state governments will be able to challenge the new order, just as some successfully did so in the lower courts, with the previous one. Lawsuits filed by states are another potential way to secure a universal (or at least very broad) injunction after Trump v. CASA, Inc.. Last year, after CASA, the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit granted one in a birthright citizenship challenging the original order.

Because the new order affects far fewer people than the original one, there may be more procedural obstacles to challenging it. But I expect eventually they will be overcome, and courts will hopefully invalidate it. There will also, of course, be wrangling about the proper scope of the resulting injunctions. I think universal injunctions are often well-justified. After Trump v. CASA, Inc., there are still various pathways to get them (or, rather, remedies very similar to them); but the Supreme Court has not so far given us definitive rulings on exactly how often those remedies are available.

The post First Legal Challenges to Trump's New Birthright Citizenship Executive Order appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: NH Federal Court Provisionally Certifies Class Of Pregnant ISIS Brides Seeking Birthright Citizenship For Their Children
articles.content:
实际上，这并没有真正发生，但《巴比伦蜜蜂》对此大有可为。

实际上，美国公民自由联盟（ACLU）已在Barbara诉特朗普案中提交了一份“澄清初步禁制令的动议”，要求法院裁定包括被认定为外国恐怖组织成员（包括宣布的敌外国人）的外国人之子女具有出生公民权。

这种声称的权力的危险性之所以加剧，是因为声称的例外范围如此模糊。行政令称，“敌外国人”被“定义为包括”行政部门指定为恐怖组织的某些群体的成员。行政令第2(a)条（强调部分）。然而，“包括”并不意味着“仅限于”。而现任行政部门已表现出愿意用极其宽松和无依据的标准，根据《敌外国人法》将个人指定为“敌外国人”。请参阅佩尔拉·特雷维佐等人，《现在他们自由了》，ProPublica（2025年7月30日），https://www.propublica.org/article/venezuelan-men-cecot-interviews-trump（描述了普通纹身在行政部门根据该法的指定中的作用）。这一已经证明的记录更加强了保护该类别免受这项非法行政令的理由。

最高法院在AARP诉特朗普案中回避了《敌外国人法》和入侵问题。我认为这起案件不会这么简单。

更难的问题是，任何州是否真的有资格主张敌外国人的权利。这样的个人数量极少，各州将很难声称任何实际的资金损失。此行政令不能被完全无效化。每一项主张都将需要分别评估。

原文《新罕布什尔联邦法院临时认证了一类寻求为其子女获得出生公民权的怀孕ISIS新娘》最初发表于Reason.com。
articles.summary:
No, that didn't actually happen, but it is ripe for the Babylon Bee.

In reality, the ACLU has filed a "motion to clarify the preliminary injunction" in Barbara v. Trump asking the court to rule that children of aliens who are members of foreign terrorist organizations, including declared Alien Enemies, are birthright citizens.

Indeed, the danger of that asserted authority is heightened because the scope of the purported exception is so unclear. The Order says that "alien enemy" is "defined to include" members of certain groups designated as terrorist organizations by the Administration. EO2 § 2(a) (emphasis added). But "include" does not mean "limited to." And this Administration has already demonstrated a willingness to use extremely loose and unfounded criteria to designate individuals as "alien enemies" purportedly under the Alien Enemies Act. See Perla Trevizo, et al., Now That They're Free, ProPublica (July 30, 2025), https://www.propublica.org/article/venezuelan-men-cecot-interviews-trump (describing the role of ordinary tattoos in the Administration's designations under the Act). That demonstrated track record is all the more reason to protect the class from this unlawful Order.

The Supreme Court ducked the Alien Enemies Act and invasion issue in AARP v. Trump. I don't think this case will be quite so simple.

The tougher question is whether any state actually has standing to assert the rights of alien enemies. The number of such individuals are so small, and states will have trouble asserting that any actual loss of funding. This executive order cannot be invalidated in its entirety. Each claim will have to be assessed separately.

The post NH Federal Court Provisionally Certifies Class Of Pregnant ISIS Brides Seeking Birthright Citizenship For Their Children appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: Justice Clarence Thomas Talking About Thomas Sowell with My Hoover Colleague Peter Robinson
articles.content: 在《索韦尔遗产》这一集中，大法官克拉伦斯·托马斯（Clarence Thomas）与彼得·罗宾逊（Peter Robinson）进行了一场广泛的对话，探讨了改变他人生轨迹的思想家。大法官托马斯回忆起自己作为年轻律师时发现托马斯·索韦尔（Thomas Sowell）作品的经历，以及随后建立的友谊，还有自立、诚实和知识独立等理念如何塑造了他的人生之路——从种族隔离的佐治亚州到美国最高法院。他们共同探讨了种族、教育、宪法主义、公共生活中的勇气，以及索韦尔的理念为何仍能引起新一代人的共鸣。
articles.summary:
In this episode of The Sowell Legacy, Justice Clarence Thomas joins Peter Robinson for a wide-ranging conversation about the thinker who transformed his life. Justice Thomas recounts discovering Thomas Sowell's work as a young lawyer, the friendship that followed, and the lessons in self-reliance, honesty, and intellectual independence that shaped his own journey—from segregated Georgia to the US Supreme Court. Together, they explore race, education, constitutionalism, courage in public life, and why Sowell's ideas continue to resonate with rising generations.

The post Justice Clarence Thomas Talking About Thomas Sowell with My Hoover Colleague Peter Robinson appeared first on Reason.com.

articles.title: The War on Drugs Has Come to the Maternity Ward
articles.content:
初看，产妇参加药物筛查似乎合情合理。为了母亲和孩子的安全，医生进行临床检测，排除任何并发症或新生儿风险的迹象。然而，故事很快变得阴暗。如果检测结果呈阳性，结果不会仅限于医生和患者之间。根据立法分析与公共政策协会的报告，在24个州和华盛顿特区，仅凭一次阳性检测就足以启动儿童福利报告。具体取决于各州，该检测可能会将母亲列入儿童虐待名单。更糟的是，母亲可能在事后才被告知检测已经进行。

这似乎违背了最高法院在费尔格森诉查尔斯顿市（2001年）的裁定，当时法院认为，在没有同意的情况下，仅以"执法目的"对孕妇进行药物检测是违宪的。然而，纽约西奈山医院的产科医生兼妇产科专家恩里玛·乌科哈（Enrima Ukoha）告诉《理性》杂志，这种被称为"检测并报告"的做法是"常见的"，"通常以非自愿的方式进行"。实际上，在过去六年中，《马歇尔计划》发现了"至少7万个案例在21个州"，父母因药物或酒精检测呈阳性而被移交执法部门。

乌科哈表示，许多医疗专业人员受到"与怀孕期间使用物质相关的刻板印象和污名化"的影响，导致他们对母亲的育儿能力做出"错误的假设"。这种做法是在应对全美阿片类药物危机的过程中发展起来的。每年，美国有近10%的出生受到药物或酒精使用的影响。

为了应对这一问题，国会修改了1974年的《儿童虐待预防和治疗法案》，使这种非自愿检测更容易发生。1974年的法律将联邦拨款与各州制定"安全护理计划"挂钩，以应对"出生并被确定为受物质滥用或戒断症状影响的"婴儿。该法案还要求涉及"交付或照顾"受影响婴儿的医疗提供者"通知儿童保护服务系统"；然而，它也规定，法律中没有任何内容应被视为要求"对任何非法行为进行起诉"。

2016年，国会通过了一项修正案，通过删去该物质滥用条款中的"非法"一词，将要求扩大到所有物质滥用的婴儿。2018年，立法者通过了另一项修正案，为这一想法提供了资金支持，授权向州机构提供补助，以"制定、更新、实施和监测"其安全护理计划。2019年，该法案再次被修订，为"出于善意报告儿童虐待或忽视"的人提供"民事和刑事责任"。

儿童虐待或忽视没有联邦定义。各州根据自己的定义制定了不同的报告和治疗标准。乌科哈表示，这一过程"在提供者、机构和各州之间存在差异"，但结果是"个体在怀孕期间未经其知情或同意进行检测"。

除了可能与新生儿分离外，母亲还面临被列入儿童虐待名单的风险，这将阻止她们从事某些职业或参加学校活动，或者面临监禁。根据CBS新闻和《马歇尔计划》的联合报告，爱达荷州的母亲尼古尔·哈曼（Nicole Hamann）因一次THC检测呈阳性，在州儿童保护名单上停留了10年。

但是，即使物质是合法的，母亲们也可能面临刑事指控。在南卡罗来纳州，艾亚娜·哈里斯-拉希德（Ayanna Harris-Rashid）因THC检测呈阳性而被捕，面临10年重罪判刑。哈里斯-拉希德承认使用CBD（该州合法，可含微量THC）来"缓解痉挛和恶心"。她的指控在被捕一年后被撤销。

与人们对这种对新生儿护理的家长式做法的看法相反，乌科哈说，目标并不是将人们与治疗联系起来，或为他们提供物质滥用资源，而是"惩罚"他们。虽然这种做法普遍存在，但多年来一直受到医学协会的谴责。美国妇产科医生学会"反对任何试图将个人行为定为犯罪的政策或做法，这些行为被指控损害其怀孕或基于怀孕结果"。

根据其医疗专业人员的意见，临床尿液检测应仅在"患者同意"的情况下进行。该指南还规定，母亲应被告知"阳性检测结果的潜在影响，包括任何强制报告要求"。此外，专家并不认为仅凭阳性药物检测结果就能证明存在物质滥用障碍，就像负检测结果也不一定排除物质使用一样。禁毒战争并未有效地阻止美国人使用毒品。如今，不知情的母亲和新生儿正通过过度热情的政策成为目标，这些政策做的一切只是扩大了犯罪阶层。
articles.summary:
At first glance, a new mother taking part in a drug screening seems reasonable. For the sake of the mother and child, a doctor performs a clinical test to rule out any complications or signs of risks to the newborn.

But the story quickly takes a dark turn. If there's a positive test result, it doesn't stay between the doctor and the patient. In 24 states and Washington, D.C., a positive test alone is enough to initiate a child welfare report, according to a report by the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association. Depending on the state, that test could land the mother on a child abuse registry. Worse still, the mother may be notified the test has occurred only after the fact.

This seems to run afoul of the Supreme Court's ruling in Ferguson v. City of Charleston (2001), where the Court found it unconstitutional to drug test pregnant women without consent solely for "law enforcement purposes." 

However, Enrima Ukoha, an obstetrician-gynecologist and maternal-fetal medicine specialist at the Mount Sinai Hospital in New York, tells Reason this practice—known as "test and report"—is "common" and "often happens in non-consensual ways." In fact, over six years, The Marshall Project found "at least 70,000 cases in 21 states" where parents were referred to law enforcement after a positive test for drug or alcohol use.

Ukoha says a lot of medical professionals are influenced by "stereotypes and stigma" associated with people who use substances in pregnancy, leading them to make "false assumptions about their ability to parent."

The practice developed as part of the response to the opioid crisis roiling the nation. Each year, nearly 10 percent of births in the U.S. are affected by drug or alcohol use. 

To deal with the issue, Congress amended the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act of 1974 in ways that made it easier for these nonconsensual tests to occur. The 1974 law ties federal grant funding to state-level development of "plans of safe care" for infants "born and identified as being affected by substance abuse or withdrawal symptoms." It also requires healthcare providers involved in the "delivery or care" of affected infants to "notify the child protective services system"; however, it also states that nothing in the law should be read as requiring "prosecution for any illegal action."

In 2016, Congress passed an amendment changing the requirement to include infants affected by all substance abuse by striking the word illegal from its substance abuse clause. In 2018, lawmakers passed another amendment that put money behind the idea, authorizing grants to assist state agencies with "developing, updating, implementing, and monitoring" their plans of safe care. And in 2019, the law was again amended to provide "civil and criminal liability" to anyone who makes a "good-faith report of child abuse or neglect."

There is no federal definition for child abuse or neglect. Left to their own devices, each state has adopted different standards for reporting and treatment. Ukoha says the process "varies across providers, institutions, and states," but the result is that "individuals are tested in pregnancy without their knowledge or consent." 

Apart from potentially being separated from their newborns, mothers risk placement on child abuse registries—which would prevent them from holding certain jobs or participating in school activities—or incarceration. In the case of Idaho mom Nicole Hamann, one positive test for THC got her 10 years on the state's child protection registry, according to a joint report by CBS News and The Marshall Project. 

But moms can find themselves facing criminal charges even when the substances are legal. In South Carolina, Ayanna Harris-Rashid was arrested and faced a 10-year felony sentence after testing positive for THC. Harris-Rashid admitted to using CBD, which is legal in the state and can contain trace amounts of THC, to "relieve cramping and nausea." Her charges were dropped a year after her arrest. 

Contrary to what one might think of this paternalist approach to neonatal care, Ukoha says the goal isn't to connect people to treatment or provide them with resources on substance abuse, but to "penalize" them.

While the practice is widespread, it's been denounced by medical associations for years. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists "opposes any policies or practices that seek to criminalize individuals for conduct alleged to be harmful to their pregnancy or based on pregnancy outcomes."

In the opinion of its medical professionals, clinical urine tests should only be performed "with the patient's consent." The guidance also states mothers should be "informed of the potential ramifications of a positive test result, including any mandatory reporting requirements." Further, experts do not consider positive drug tests alone to be proof of a substance abuse disorder, just as a negative test wouldn't necessarily rule out substance use. 

The war on drugs has not meaningfully deterred Americans from using drugs. Now, unassuming mothers and their newborns are being targeted through overzealous policies that do nothing but expand the criminal class.

The post The War on Drugs Has Come to the Maternity Ward appeared first on Reason.com.
